title: THE TREE THAT LOOKED ALIVE… UNTIL JESUS CAME CLOSE ENOUGH TO SEE THE TRUTH
paragraphs: THE TREE THAT LOOKED ALIVE… UNTIL JESUS CAME CLOSE ENOUGH TO SEE THE TRUTH

The Terrifying Lesson of the Fig Tree: You Can Have the Appearance of a Thriving Christian, Know All the Right Scriptures, and Convince Everyone You're Spiritually Alive—Yet Be Hiding a Barrenness That Only Jesus Can See.
There is something terrifying about a tree that looks alive from a distance.
Not because its branches are broken.
Not because its leaves are falling.
Not because everyone can see that something is wrong.
But because everything about it suggests that it is healthy.
Its leaves are green. Its branches are spreading. Its appearance promises life.
And yet, when someone comes close enough to look for fruit…
There is nothing.
Now imagine something even more unsettling.
What if that tree is not growing beside a dusty road in ancient Israel?
What if that tree is sitting in church every Sunday?
What if it knows worship songs by heart, shares Bible verses on Facebook, says “God bless you” to everyone, and knows exactly when to raise its hands during prayer?
What if that tree has been baptized, has served in ministry, and has spent years being called a faithful Christian?
What if that tree…
Is you?
Before you become offended, before you reassure yourself that this message must be for someone else, there is something you need to understand.
Jesus once approached a fig tree that looked promising from a distance.
What happened next was so disturbing that His disciples remembered it.
And what He revealed through that moment still confronts every person who has learned how to look spiritually alive without actually living in surrender to God.
Because one of the most dangerous places a human soul can occupy is not open rebellion against God.
It is religious confidence without genuine repentance.
It is knowing how to perform Christianity while slowly losing intimacy with Christ.
It is becoming so comfortable with the appearance of spiritual life that you stop asking whether the Holy Spirit is actually transforming you.
And the frightening part?
You can fool a congregation.
You can fool your family.
You can even deceive yourself.
But you cannot fool the One who comes looking for fruit.
The story begins in Mark 11.
Jesus had entered Jerusalem during the final week before His crucifixion. The crowds had welcomed Him with cries of “Hosanna!” They had spread cloaks and leafy branches along His path.
From the outside, Jerusalem was filled with religious excitement.
There were celebrations, prayers, sacrifices, and a magnificent temple.
Everything looked alive.
But Jesus saw what appearances could not reveal.
Mark tells us that the following day, as Jesus and His disciples were leaving Bethany, He became hungry.
Then Scripture says:
“Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.”
— Mark 11:13, ESV
Read that again.
Nothing but leaves.
Three words that should make every professing Christian examine their heart.
The tree was not described as dead.
It was not described as withered.
It was not described as incapable of producing fruit.
It was covered in leaves.
It appeared to offer something that it did not actually possess.
And there is an important historical detail here.

Fig trees in that region could develop small, early edible growth before or alongside their mature leaves, even though the main fig harvest came later. A leafy tree could therefore invite an expectation of some early fruit.
Mark explicitly tells us that it was not the regular season for figs. We must not erase that detail to make the story easier.
The point is not that Jesus was irrationally demanding a full harvest out of season.
The unusual timing, the tree's leafy appearance, and the surrounding events invite us to recognize a prophetic sign.
Jesus was not simply giving an agricultural lesson.
He was exposing something much deeper.
And the placement of this story in Mark's Gospel is crucial.
Jesus encounters the tree, enters the temple and confronts its corruption, and then the disciples discover that the tree has withered.
The events interpret one another.
The temple was supposed to be a place of prayer.
Jesus declared:
“Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.”
— Mark 11:17, ESV; drawing from Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11
The temple was bustling with activity, but its religious activity was not the same as faithfulness to God.
There was an outward appearance of devotion, yet Jesus exposed serious spiritual corruption.
The fig tree became a visible warning about the danger of fruitless religion.

And before anyone uses this passage to condemn an entire people, remember that Jesus Himself was Jewish, His earliest disciples were Jewish, and His confrontation was directed toward genuine covenant faithfulness, not ethnic superiority.
The warning reaches every generation that claims to know God.
Including ours.
Including our churches.
Including you and me.
Because it is possible to build a Christian identity so convincing that nobody notices how far your private life has drifted from the Jesus you publicly proclaim.
You can post about forgiveness while refusing to forgive the person who wounded you.
You can quote Scripture about love while treating your spouse with contempt.
You can lead worship on Sunday and spend Monday destroying someone's reputation.
You can write beautiful prayers in public while barely speaking to God when nobody is watching.
You can give money, attend conferences, serve in ministries, and memorize entire passages of Scripture.
And still resist the voice of the Holy Spirit when He confronts your pride, bitterness, dishonesty, or unbelief.
Please understand.
None of those outward religious activities is automatically wrong.
Worship matters.
Church fellowship matters.
Giving matters.
Serving matters.
Studying Scripture matters.
But religious activities cannot substitute for a living relationship with Jesus Christ.
The danger begins when we use good things to hide the absence of the most important thing.
We become so busy doing things associated with Jesus that we neglect abiding in Jesus Himself.
And eventually, we mistake movement for maturity.
Attention for anointing.
Knowledge for obedience.
Popularity for faithfulness.
Ministry success for spiritual health.
Leaves for fruit.
There is a Greek expression in Mark 11:13 that makes this confrontation especially vivid.
The Gospel says:
οὐδὲν εὗρεν εἰ μὴ φύλλα
Ouden heuren ei mē phylla.
“He found nothing except leaves.”
The phrase is straightforward, but its simplicity is devastating.
Nothing.
Except.
Leaves.
There was something visible.
But what was visible did not provide what was being sought.
And perhaps that is the question you have been avoiding.
If Jesus examined your life beyond what other people can see, what would He find?
Not your Christian biography.
Not your Facebook posts.
Not your ministry title.
Not the number of years you have attended church.
Not the reputation you have carefully maintained.
Your actual life.
Your private choices.
Your treatment of people who cannot benefit you.
Your response when Scripture contradicts your desires.
Your willingness to confess wrongdoing when it costs you your pride.
Your obedience when nobody applauds.
Your trust in God when prayers remain unanswered.
Your love for the people who are difficult to love.
Would He find a heart that is increasingly becoming like His?
Or would He find an impressive collection of religious leaves?
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us are not pretending to be Christians.
We genuinely believe in Jesus.
We love hearing His Word.
We remember seasons when prayer felt alive, worship brought tears to our eyes, and obedience mattered more than approval.
But something happened along the way.
Perhaps disappointment hardened your heart.
Perhaps a betrayal made you suspicious of everyone.
Perhaps an unanswered prayer caused you to withdraw from God.
Perhaps success made you self-sufficient.
Perhaps a hidden sin slowly became a familiar companion.
Perhaps you were wounded by people who claimed to represent Christ, and without realizing it, you began distancing yourself from Christ Himself.
You did not wake up one morning announcing that you wanted to become spiritually barren.
It happened gradually.
One neglected prayer.
One postponed confession.
One compromise rationalized.
One act of forgiveness refused.
One conviction silenced.
One season of spiritual dryness that you never brought honestly before God.
And the frightening thing about gradual spiritual decline is that your outward life can remain remarkably unchanged.
You still know the songs.
You still remember the verses.
You still know how to smile at church.
You still know how to tell people, “I'm blessed.”
But somewhere beneath the leaves, your soul is struggling.
You are exhausted from maintaining an appearance of strength while privately wondering why you feel so distant from God.
If that describes you, please keep reading.
Because the story of the fig tree is not merely a warning about judgment.
Read within the larger Gospel, it also drives us toward the only One who can give us true life.
But first, we need to confront something modern Christianity sometimes tries desperately to avoid.
Jesus does not measure spiritual life by appearances.
In Matthew 7:16, Jesus says:
“You will recognize them by their fruits.”
The Greek word translated “fruits” is καρποί (karpoi), the plural of karpos, meaning fruit or produce.
In context, Jesus is warning about false prophets, whose outward appearance can conceal their true character.
His words establish a wider principle: what a person consistently produces reveals something about the life and loyalties beneath the surface.
And Galatians 5:22–23 tells us what the Spirit's fruit looks like:
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Patience.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Gentleness.
Self-control.
Notice what is not on that list.
Followers.
Views.
Applause.
A religious title.
A perfect-looking family photograph.
An impressive ministry platform.
A reputation for knowing the Bible better than everyone else.
Those things cannot prove that the Holy Spirit is transforming someone's heart.
You can be deeply admired by people and still need to repent before God.
You can have almost no public recognition and still be quietly bearing beautiful spiritual fruit.
Think about the mother who is exhausted but chooses patience with her children.
The husband who finally admits that his harsh words have wounded his wife and begins seeking forgiveness.
The young believer who refuses to join friends in humiliating someone who is not present.
The employee who tells the truth even when dishonesty would be profitable.
The wounded person who begins the difficult journey of forgiveness without pretending the harm never happened.
The person battling temptation who stops hiding, confesses, seeks accountability, and returns to Christ.
The elderly believer who prays faithfully for people who may never know her name.
Those lives may never become viral.
But they matter deeply to God.
Because spiritual fruit is not always spectacular.
Sometimes it looks like an apology.
Sometimes it looks like restraint.
Sometimes it looks like generosity without recognition.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth after years of lying.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to retaliate when you have every opportunity.
Sometimes it looks like a trembling prayer whispered through tears:
“Jesus, I cannot keep living this way. Please change me.”
And perhaps that prayer is closer to genuine spiritual life than a thousand polished religious performances.
But we need to be careful here.
The message of the fig tree is not that Christians must achieve flawless moral performance to earn God's love.
That would distort the Gospel.
Jesus did not come to save people who had already made themselves spiritually fruitful.
He came to save sinners.
He came for the guilty.
The ashamed.
The hypocritical.
The wounded.
The rebellious.
The people who have spent years hiding behind appearances.
He came for people who could never rescue themselves.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our works.
And the very next verse, Ephesians 2:10, explains that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because we have produced enough fruit.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ, and His transforming work produces fruit in our lives.
Fruit is not the price of salvation.
It is the evidence of a life being changed by grace.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because if you misunderstand it, you will either become proud of your religious achievements or crushed by your spiritual failures.
But the Gospel destroys both pride and despair.
It tells the proud person, “You cannot save yourself.”
And it tells the broken person, “You do not have to save yourself.”
Jesus Christ is sufficient.
And now we arrive at one of the most sobering moments in the entire account.
Jesus speaks to the tree:
“May no one ever eat fruit from you again.”
— Mark 11:14, ESV
The following morning, Peter notices that the tree has withered from its roots.
From its roots.
Not merely a few fallen leaves.
Not simply a damaged branch.
The tree's condition had changed at the very source of its life.
And this should remind us that outward appearances cannot sustain what is spiritually empty.
You can decorate a dying tree.
You can tie beautiful ribbons around its branches.
You can illuminate it with expensive lights.
You can place it in the center of a celebration.
But decoration cannot create life.
In the same way, no amount of religious performance can regenerate a human heart.
Only God can give spiritual life.
Only Christ can reconcile sinners to the Father.
Only the Holy Spirit can produce the fruit that reflects His character.
This is why Jesus' words in John 15 are so important.
He says:
“I am the vine; you are the branches.”
— John 15:5, ESV
The Greek expression begins:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος
Egō eimi hē ampelos.
“I am the vine.”
Jesus does not say, “I am the decoration.”
He does not say, “I am the religious accessory you add to an otherwise self-sufficient life.”
He identifies Himself as the essential source of the branches' fruitfulness.
And then He says:
“Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit.”
— John 15:5, ESV
The Greek verb μένω (menō), translated “abide” or “remain,” communicates continuing, staying, or remaining.
It is not describing a momentary religious emotion.
It is pointing toward an ongoing relationship of dependence upon Christ.
That is where true spiritual fruit comes from.
Not from trying harder to impress God.
Not from creating a more convincing Christian image.
Not from comparing yourself with people whose struggles look worse than yours.
But from remaining in Jesus through faith, receiving His Word, depending on His grace, and responding to Him in obedience.
You cannot manufacture the fruit of the Spirit through public relations.
You cannot edit spiritual maturity into your life like a photograph.
You cannot purchase holiness.
You cannot inherit repentance from your parents.
You cannot borrow intimacy with Christ from your pastor.
You must personally come to Jesus.
And this is where the story should make us uncomfortable for another reason.
Some of us are more concerned about being exposed than being healed.
We fear someone discovering our hidden sin more than we grieve the sin itself.
We fear losing our reputation more than losing our sensitivity to God's Word.
We want forgiveness without confession.
Restoration without repentance.
Peace without surrender.
We want Jesus to protect our image while leaving our idols untouched.
But Jesus loves us too deeply to call spiritual emptiness spiritual health.
His truth confronts us because sin is destructive.
And His grace invites us to turn because His mercy is real.
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It refers to repentance, a genuine turning of heart and life, not merely feeling embarrassed because wrongdoing has been discovered.
Biblical repentance is more than emotional regret.
It involves recognizing sin as sin, turning toward God, and responding to His truth.
It is not the attempt to buy forgiveness through enough tears.
It is the honest response of someone who stops defending what God is calling them to surrender.
And perhaps the most courageous prayer you could offer tonight is not an eloquent prayer.
Perhaps it is simply:
“Lord, I have been pretending.”
No excuses.
No performance.
No attempt to blame everyone else.
Just honesty before the Savior who already knows.
“Jesus, I have been more concerned with appearing faithful than actually obeying You.”
“Jesus, I have allowed bitterness to grow inside me.”
“Jesus, I know the Scriptures, but I have resisted what they require of me.”
“Jesus, I am tired of hiding.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There is something profoundly beautiful about the moment a person stops trying to impress God and begins telling Him the truth.
Because He was never deceived by the performance.
And He is not surprised by the confession.
Consider the apostle Peter.
He promised extraordinary loyalty to Jesus.
He believed he would remain faithful even if everyone else abandoned Him.
But when pressure came, Peter denied knowing his Lord.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
The sound of the rooster.
The realization that his courage had collapsed.
The bitter weeping.
Peter had discovered that his confidence in himself was much greater than his actual strength.
But his failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
The man who denied Jesus became a witness to the risen Christ.
Not because Peter's denial was insignificant.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
But because the mercy of Jesus is greater than the failure of a repentant sinner.
That is the Gospel.
And this is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not simply about exposing spiritual barrenness.
It is about the Savior who can transform a life that seemed hopeless.
From denial to restoration.
From self-righteousness to surrender.
From hidden sin to honest repentance.
From empty religion to living faith.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing every earthly consequence of our choices.
But by forgiving sinners, reconciling them to God, giving them new life, and teaching them to walk in truth.
And if you are wondering whether your own story has gone too far for restoration, listen carefully.
Your past may explain your wounds.
It does not have the authority to declare Christ powerless to redeem you.
Your failure may have consequences.
It does not mean you are beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Your spiritual dryness may be real.
It does not mean you should stop seeking the One who gives living water.
There is another fig tree passage that helps us hold judgment and mercy together.
In Luke 13:6–9, Jesus tells a parable about a fig tree that has failed to produce fruit.
The owner wants it removed.
But the gardener asks for additional time to cultivate and fertilize it.
He hopes that it will yet bear fruit.
This is a different passage with a different setting from Mark 11, and we should not pretend the two stories are identical.
Yet together, they confront us with the seriousness of fruitlessness and the urgency of responding to mercy.
God's patience must never be mistaken for permission to remain unrepentant.
And His warnings must never be separated from His gracious invitation to turn to Him.
The fact that you are hearing a call to repentance today is not a reason to despair.
It is a reason to respond.
Do not wait until your conscience becomes harder.
Do not wait until the hidden habit has damaged another relationship.
Do not wait until the bitterness has shaped your entire personality.
Do not wait until your children learn from your example that Christianity is merely a public performance.
Do not wait for a crisis to become honest with God.
Come to Jesus now.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
But because He is worthy of your trust.
And because He has already done what you could never accomplish for yourself.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God gave His life for sinners.
He bore the judgment that our sin deserved.
He was crucified, buried, and raised from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed.
The cross is not a religious decoration.
It is the place where the seriousness of sin and the greatness of divine love meet.
Romans 5:8 says:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
— ESV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we achieved spiritual perfection.
Not after we learned how to look respectable.
While we were still sinners.
That is why the Gospel is good news for the person who has been hiding behind leaves.
Jesus already knows what is beneath them.
And He still calls sinners to repent and believe.
There is no need to defend your false appearance before the One who can give you a new heart.
There is no need to cling to a religious mask when the Savior offers something far greater than an improved reputation.
He offers forgiveness.
He offers reconciliation.
He offers new life.
He offers Himself.
And if you belong to Christ, He does not abandon the work He has begun in you.
Philippians 1:6 expresses Paul's confidence that God will complete His good work in His people.
That does not mean every believer grows at the same speed.
It does not mean Christians never struggle.
It does not mean a painful season of grief, depression, exhaustion, or spiritual dryness automatically proves that someone is spiritually barren.
Please do not confuse suffering with hypocrisy.
A bruised believer who is clinging to Christ may be bearing more genuine fruit than a confident religious performer who has no desire to obey Him.
Sometimes fruit grows quietly.
Sometimes growth happens through tears.
Sometimes faithfulness is simply refusing to abandon Jesus when everything in your life feels heavy.
A struggling Christian is not necessarily a fruitless Christian.
The question is not whether you have experienced weakness.
The question is whether you are willing to bring your weakness into the light of Christ and remain dependent on Him.
And there is something else you need to hear.
You do not need to pretend that you are already healed to be welcomed into the process of healing.
You do not need to claim victory over every temptation before asking for prayer.
You do not need to hide your grief to prove that you trust God.
You do not need to perform happiness to demonstrate that the Holy Spirit lives in you.
You can be honest.
You can ask for help.
You can confess.
You can seek wise pastoral care, accountability, and professional support when appropriate.
You can make restitution where possible.
You can take concrete steps to repair what your sin has damaged.
You can return to Scripture, not as a religious trophy, but as God's Word that reveals His truth.
You can pray again, even if the first prayer is barely more than a whisper.
And you can trust that genuine growth is not measured by how impressive you look tomorrow morning.
It is measured by the transforming work of God over a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
Perhaps someone reading this has not prayed sincerely in months.
Perhaps your Bible has remained unopened while your social media has been filled with Christian quotations.
Perhaps you have been encouraging strangers online while neglecting the people who need your love at home.
Perhaps you are serving in a church but privately carrying resentment toward its members.
Perhaps you have been sharing messages about repentance while refusing to acknowledge your own wrongdoing.
If that is you, this moment does not have to end in shame.
It can become a turning point.
Not because an article has supernatural power.
Not because emotion itself produces salvation.
But because the Word of God calls us to the living Christ, and the Holy Spirit uses His truth to convict, awaken, and transform.
You can close this article and return to the same patterns.
Or you can respond honestly to what God has shown you.
You can speak to the person you need to apologize to.
You can confess the sin you have been protecting.
You can stop nurturing the bitterness you have justified for years.
You can seek accountability instead of relying on secrecy.
You can return to the Savior whose mercy you have been afraid to approach.
And you can begin again—not by trusting your determination to be perfect, but by trusting Jesus Christ.
There is a Hebrew prayer that captures this longing beautifully.
In Psalm 51:10, David cries out:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
— Psalm 51:10, ESV
The Hebrew verb בְּרָא (bera) comes from bara, “to create.”
David was not asking God to improve his public image.
He was asking God to work within him.
To cleanse what sin had corrupted.
To renew what he could not repair through religious performance.
That is the prayer we need.
Not “Lord, make everyone think I am holy.”
But “Lord, make my heart clean.”
Not “Lord, help me hide my failures.”
But “Lord, teach me to walk in the truth.”
Not “Lord, give me a larger platform.”
But “Lord, make me faithful with the life You have entrusted to me.”
Not “Lord, let me appear fruitful.”
But “Lord, let my life genuinely bear fruit that glorifies You.”
Because the world does not need another generation of Christians who are experts at appearing righteous while refusing to be transformed.
It needs believers who are humble enough to repent.
Courageous enough to tell the truth.
Tender enough to love.
Faithful enough to obey when obedience is costly.
And honest enough to say, “I still need Jesus every single day.”
This is the kind of discipleship we want to cultivate at Gospel Warrior.
Not shallow religious excitement that disappears when life becomes difficult.
Not a Christianity built around appearances, arguments, or applause.
But deep roots in Scripture.
A growing understanding of the Gospel.
A willingness to confront sin with truth and grace.
A community that encourages spiritual growth rather than pretending that everyone has already arrived.
And practical resources that help believers continue learning long after an emotional moment has passed.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their understanding of biblical truth, grow in prayer, and pursue a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
And we want you to invite others into that opportunity.
Your family.
Your friends.
The believer who feels spiritually exhausted.
The person who has stopped attending church.
The Christian who has become comfortable with compromise.
The seeker who has questions about Jesus.
Even the unbeliever who may be willing to discover what the Gospel actually teaches.
Because spiritual growth should never be reduced to a private religious performance.
We are called to encourage one another toward love and good works.
And if this message has confronted you, do not let it become another article you read, feel deeply for a moment, and then forget.
And if you have experienced the mercy of Christ after a season of failure, consider sharing a short testimony of what His grace has done in your life.
You do not need to reveal private details or publicly confess something that should be addressed with a trusted pastor, counselor, or affected person.
But your honest words may help someone else understand that they are not alone in their struggle.
Someone reading the comments may be one prayer away from admitting they need help.
Someone may be afraid to return to church.
Someone may believe their failures have disqualified them from ever being loved by God.
Let your response point them toward Jesus.
Not simply to increase the number of people who see a post.
But because someone in your circle may be carrying a spiritual burden you know nothing about.
That person may never tell you what they are going through.
They may never publicly acknowledge that this message reached them.
But God's Word can still confront and encourage them.
And if you believe in this mission and have the financial ability to help sustain it, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Not because paying a monthly fee proves that you are more spiritual than someone who cannot afford it.
And certainly not because giving money is a requirement for salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual fruitfulness.
Those claims would contradict the Gospel we are committed to proclaiming.
But Scripture does teach the importance of generous, willing support for ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loves a cheerful giver.”
The verse also teaches that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion.
That matters.
Christian generosity is meant to flow from grace, not fear.

In the Old Testament, tithes and offerings were part of Israel's covenant life and worship. Christians differ in how they understand the continuing application of the tithe, but the New Testament clearly encourages willing, proportionate, generous giving.
It should not replace your responsibilities to your household or the giving commitments you prayerfully make to your local church.
And it should never be understood as buying spiritual blessings.
It can help us continue producing Scripture-anchored articles, devotionals, teaching resources, and discipleship materials.
It can help us pursue the vision of making biblical encouragement accessible to more people.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
Helping people understand Scripture and grow as disciples of Christ is.
You are still welcome.
You can still read, pray, learn, share, comment, and grow alongside us.
Your worth before God is not measured by your financial contribution.
And your ability to glorify God is not limited to monetary giving.
You can glorify Him through faithful obedience, love, generosity, prayer, service, and sharing His truth.
If you cannot, your prayers and thoughtful sharing are meaningful ways to encourage this work.
The goal is not to build an impressive religious platform covered in leaves.
The goal is to serve Christ faithfully and help people encounter the truth of His Gospel.
And that brings us back to the road outside Jerusalem.
Back to the fig tree.
Back to the leaves.
Back to the moment Jesus approached something that appeared fruitful but was not.
Can you imagine standing there with the disciples?
Watching the Lord examine that tree.
Hearing His words.
Returning the following morning and seeing its withered condition.
Then remembering that the same Jesus who spoke judgment over the tree would soon be arrested, condemned, and crucified.
The One who exposed fruitlessness would go to the cross for sinners.
The One who confronted religious hypocrisy would give His life so that hypocrites, rebels, and broken people could be forgiven and transformed.
The One who warned about judgment would bear the cost of redemption for those who trust in Him.
And three days after His burial, the tomb would be empty.
Death would not have the final word.
Sin would not have the final word.
Human failure would not have the final word.
The risen Christ would.
That is why this article cannot end merely by telling you to produce more fruit.
It must end by pointing you to Jesus.
Because if all you hear is “Try harder,” you may simply grow more religious leaves.
You may become more disciplined at hiding.
More skilled at performing.
More anxious about being exposed.
But if you hear the Gospel, you will understand that the answer to spiritual barrenness is not another layer of appearance.
It is repentance and living faith in Christ.
It is returning to the Vine.
It is trusting the Savior.
It is allowing His Word to confront you and His grace to change you.
It is receiving His mercy with humility and walking in the newness of life He provides.
And perhaps tonight, for the first time in a long time, you will stop asking:
“Do people think I am a good Christian?”
And begin asking:
“Lord Jesus, am I truly abiding in You?”
That question can change everything.
Because one day, your reputation will no longer matter.
The applause will stop.
The notifications will disappear.
The titles will be forgotten.
The carefully maintained image will no longer protect you.
And what will matter is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Not whether you were admired.
Not whether you were famous.
Not whether you looked spiritually impressive.
But whether you knew the Savior and were known by Him.
So before you move on to another post, another video, another distraction, I invite you to pray.
“Lord Jesus, You know me completely.
You know the parts of my life that people admire, and You know the parts I have tried to hide.
Forgive me for the times I have valued religious appearances more than obedience to You.
Forgive my pride, my hypocrisy, my unbelief, and the sins I have excused.
I cannot cleanse my own heart.
I cannot save myself.
I need Your mercy.
Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again.
Teach me to abide in You.
Produce in my life the fruit of Your Spirit.
Give me courage to repent where I have been wrong, humility to seek forgiveness where I have caused harm, and faith to trust You when I feel weak.
Make me a person who loves You not only with words, but with a life increasingly surrendered to Your truth.
And let whatever good comes from my life bring glory to You, not to me.
In Your holy name, Jesus.
Amen.”
If you prayed that sincerely, do not measure the reality of your response by whether you felt a dramatic emotion.
Continue seeking Christ.
Open His Word.
Find faithful Christian fellowship.
Ask for prayer.
Make the changes repentance requires.
And remember that a genuine life of faith is not sustained by a single emotional moment, but by the grace of God as you continue trusting and following Jesus.
Now, before you leave, ask yourself one final question.
If Jesus came close enough to examine the life behind your leaves, would you want Him to find a perfect performance…
Or a surrendered heart that truly belongs to Him?
Choose the truth.
Choose repentance.
Choose the Savior who gives life.
And never forget:
The most tragic tree is not the one whose leaves have fallen, but the one so covered in leaves that nobody notices its fruit is missing—until Jesus comes looking.
